tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead, an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No "@", no leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no "@" anywhere, no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

## 1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai .../artifact/... link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{...}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

content.content: === qr-scanner README worker/vite notes 1-# QR Scanner 2- 3:Javascript QR Code Scanner based on [Cosmo Wolfe's javascript port](https://github.com/cozmo/jsqr) of [Google's ZXing library](https://github.com/zxing/zxing). 4- 5-In this library, several improvements have been applied over the original port: 6- 7-- Web cam scanning support out of the box 8:- Uses the browser's native [BarcodeDetector](https://web.dev/shape-detection/) [if available](https://github.com/WICG/shape-detection-api#overview) 9-- Lightweight: ~59.3 kB (~16.3 kB gzipped) minified with Google's closure compiler. If the native `BarcodeDetector` is available, only ~15.3 kB (~5.6 kB gzipped) are loaded. 10-- Improved performance and reduced memory footprint. 11:- Runs in a WebWorker which keeps the main / UI thread responsive. 12-- Can be configured for better performance on colored QR codes. 13- 14:According to [our benchmarking](https://github.com/danimoh/qr-scanner-benchmark) this project's scanner engine's detection rate is about 2-3 times (and up to 8 times) as high as the one of the most popular javascript QR scanner library [LazarSoft/jsqrcode](https://github.com/LazarSoft/jsqrcode). Also the other library oftentimes misreads the content of QR codes, while for this project no misreads occurred in the benchmarking. 15- 16-The library supports scanning a continuous video stream from a web cam as well as scanning of single images. 17- 18:The development of this library is sponsored by [nimiq](https://www.nimiq.com), world's first browser based blockchain. 19- 20:[](https://nimiq.com) 21- 22- 23-## Demo 24:See [https://nimiq.github.io/qr-scanner/demo/](https://nimiq.github.io/qr-scanner/demo/) 25- 26-## Installation 27- 28-To install via npm: 29-```bash 30-npm install --save qr-scanner -- 34-yarn add qr-scanner 35-``` 36:Or simply copy `qr-scanner.min.js` and `qr-scanner-worker.min.js` to your project. 37- 38-## Setup 39- 40:The QR Scanner consists of two main files. `qr-scanner.min.js` is the main API file which loads the worker script `qr-scanner-worker.min.js` via a dynamic import, only if needed. If you are not using a bundler like Rollup or Webpack that handles dynamic imports automatically, you might have to copy `qr-scanner-worker.min.js` over to your dist, next to `qr-scanner.min.js` or next to the script into which you're bundling `qr-scanner.min.js`. 41- 42-`qr-scanner.min.js` is an es6 module and can be imported as follows: 43-```js 44:import QrScanner from 'path/to/qr-scanner.min.js'; // if using plain es6 import 45:import QrScanner from 'qr-scanner'; // if installed via package and bundling with a module bundler like webpack or rollup 46-``` 47-This requires the importing script to also be an es6 module or a module script tag, e.g.: 48-```html 49- 53-``` 54- 55-If your project is not based on es6 modules you can 56:- use a [dynamic import](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/import#Dynamic_Imports) to import the es6 module: 57-```js 58-import('path/to/qr-scanner.min.js').then((module) => { 59- const QrScanner = module.default; 60- // do something with QrScanner 61-}); 62-``` 63:- use the [UMD build](https://github.com/umdjs/umd) `qr-scanner.umd.min.js` for direct usage as non-module script 64-```html 65- 66- 69-``` 70:- bundle `qr-scanner.umd.min.js` directly with your non-module code with tools like [gulp](https://gulpjs.com/) or [grunt](https://gruntjs.com/). 71:- bundle the lib with `require` based bundlers like [browserify](https://browserify.org/): 72-```js 73-const QrScanner = require('qr-scanner'); // if installed via package 74-const QrScanner = require('path/to/qr-scanner.umd.min.js'); // if not installed via package 75-// do something with QrScanner 76-``` 77- 78:This library uses ECMAScript 2017 features like `async` functions. If you need to support old browsers, you can use `qr-scanner.legacy.min.js`, which is ECMAScript 2015 (ES6) compatible. It's a UMD build and can be used as a replacement for `qr-scanner.umd.min.js`, see above. Note, that the legacy build is larger as it includes some polyfills and, to support browsers that don't support dynamic imports, inlines the worker script which however would be needed to be loaded in legacy browsers anyway. You will likely not need to use the legacy build though, as general browser support is already very good for the regular build. Especially if you want to scan from the device's camera, camera support by the browser is the stricter restriction. 79- 80-## Usage 81- 82-### Web Cam Scanning 83- 84-#### 1. entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.

- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

- **User gesture:** The permission dialog can only be brought up from a user gesture (tap/click), and a prior grant lets you call it again without interaction.

Possible next step: test on a real device with a certificate the device trusts (for example, a locally installed CA or a tunnel with a valid certificate). Then check whether `window.isSecureContext` is true and whether `requestPermission` resolves to `granted`. This would separate the certificate trust question from the gesture and worker issues.

ngrok's free-tier interstitial is a known problem for browser-based clients, and the docs list a few ways around it.

- **Why it appears:** ngrok adds the page in front of HTML browser traffic on the free tier to counter phishing. After a user agrees, ngrok sets a cookie that lasts seven days for that domain.
- **The header fix:** ngrok's error page says the warning can be skipped by sending the `ngrok-skip-browser-warning` request header with any value, or by sending a custom non-standard User-Agent (). The same page also lists upgrading to a paid account as an option.
- **Limits of the fix:** The header has to come from the client making the request. Adding it in your server's response doesn't work, since a middleware that sets the header on the app side still showed the page, and a commenter explains that the warning is returned at the edge, outside the app's control. ngrok's Traffic Policy add-headers action also can't be used for this header ().
- **Relevance to Claude.ai:** A GitHub issue on the MCP project reports that iframe-originated asset requests from Claude.ai don't include this header, so they receive the interstitial HTML instead of the expected JS/CSS. That makes widget rendering fail, and the issue proposes adding the header to iframe requests.
- **Developer workarounds:** Some developers add the header with a browser extension. One forum reply says they use the ModHeader extension with the header to solve the same problem, and another suggests Requestly with a rule for `*.ngrok-free.app` ().

Bottom line: on current docs, active WebSocket traffic keeps a free service awake. Any 5-minute drops or restarts you see may be the older issue or a separate restart, so test your own service.

The results support the core problem, but none of them mention `visibilitychange` or socket.io specifically.

- **Background sockets get closed by iOS.** One Apple developer thread reports that when Safari goes to the background, the server sees the client leave and closes the socket. On return to the foreground, the page gets error and close events and can reconnect. When Safari is switched to the background the websocket server recognizes the client going away and closes the websocket. When Safari gets to the foreground again, onerror and onclose events are received which allow my site to re-establish the connection.
- **Close events can go missing.** The same thread says that after longer inactivity the error and close events stopped arriving, so the page could not detect the dead connection. A WebKit bug report describes a similar case, where the socket looked open after a network drop and no close event fired.
- **readyState can lie.** A well-known gist reports that inside `onmessage` the `readyState` can still read open even though the socket is closed, and that calling `send()` then can crash Safari. Deferring the send with `setTimeout` avoids this. The gist also notes that the onclose event is fired after the onmessage events.

content.content:
**What is restored**
- Connection state recovery "allows restoring a client's state after a temporary disconnection, including any missed packets."
- After an unexpected disconnection, the server stores "the `id`, the rooms and the `data` attribute of the socket." Manual disconnects via `socket.disconnect()` are excluded.
- Missed events are delivered on reconnect: "any event missed during the disconnection period will be received now."

**Server options**
- `connectionStateRecovery` must be enabled explicitly on the server.
- `maxDisconnectionDuration`: "the backup duration of the sessions and the packets." The example value is `2 * 60 * 1000`. The docs advise a sensible value, not `Infinity`.
- `skipMiddlewares`: "whether to skip middlewares upon successful recovery." The example value is `false`.
- The page does not state default values for either option.

**When recovery may not work**
- The docs say "the recovery will not always be successful," so clients must still handle unsynchronized state.
- The feature targets intermittent disconnections, so a finite `maxDisconnectionDuration` is needed.
- The Redis adapter does not support recovery, since persisting packets "is not compatible with the Redis PUB/SUB mechanism."
- The server must send at least one event so the client can initialize its offset.
- The page does not mention page reloads, server restarts, or exceeding the maximum duration as specific cases.

**`socket.recovered`**
- "The `recovered` attribute indicates whether this recovery was successful." It is available on the server socket and the client socket.

**Volatile packets and acknowledgements**
- The page does not mention volatile packets or acknowledgements, so it says nothing about whether they are stored.

The official Socket.IO docs support the core of your premise: websocket-only transport avoids the sticky-session requirement, but gives up polling fallback. I found no source that recommends websocket-first as a general default.

- **Why sticky sessions exist:** The official docs say that polling sends several HTTP requests over a session's life, so requests for one session ID must reach the same process. content.content:
The potentially-trustworthy decision is made in these functions:

- **`shouldTreatAsPotentiallyTrustworthy(StringView protocol, StringView host)`**, the core check, which returns true if any of four conditions holds:
  - `if (LegacySchemeRegistry::shouldTreatURLSchemeAsSecure(protocol))`
  - `if (SecurityOrigin::isLocalHostOrLoopbackIPAddress(host))`
  - `if (LegacySchemeRegistry::shouldTreatURLSchemeAsLocal(protocol))`
  - `if (LegacySchemeRegistry::schemeIsHandledBySchemeHandler(protocol))`
- **`shouldTreatAsPotentiallyTrustworthy(const URL& url)`**, a wrapper that passes the URL's protocol and host to the core check.
- **`SecurityOrigin::isPotentiallyTrustworthy() const`**, which caches the result: `m_isPotentiallyTrustworthy = shouldTreatAsPotentiallyTrustworthy(m_data.protocol(), m_data.host());`
- **`isLoopbackIPAddress(StringView host)`**, which accepts `[::1]` (`if (host == "[::1]"_s)`) and hosts beginning with `127.` that contain exactly three dots and only digits otherwise.
- **`SecurityOrigin::isLocalHostOrLoopbackIPAddress`** and **`isLocalhostAddress`**, which accept `localhost` and any host ending in `.localhost`: `return equalLettersIgnoringASCIICase(host, "localhost"_s) || host.endsWithIgnoringASCIICase(".localhost"_s);`

**Certificate validity:** None of these functions checks the TLS certificate. They never inspect certificates, chains, expiry, or revocation. Trustworthiness is determined only by the URL's scheme and host.

**Schemes:** The code does not hard-code `https`, `wss`, or `file` in these functions. Scheme classification is delegated to `LegacySchemeRegistry`, whose contents are not included in this excerpt, so I can't confirm which schemes it lists. The related `SecurityOrigin::isSecure(const URL&)` similarly treats invalid URLs as secure, delegates secure schemes to the registry, and routes `blob:` URLs to `BlobURL::isSecureBlobURL`.

**Volatile events**

content.content:
**Message ordering**
- "Socket.IO does guarantee message ordering, no matter which low-level transport is used"
- Order holds even when upgrading from HTTP long-polling to WebSocket, based on TCP guarantees and the upgrade design.

**At most once (default)**
- "By default, Socket.IO provides an **at most once** guarantee of delivery"
- If the connection breaks mid-send, the sender can't know whether the event arrived, and there's no retry on reconnection: "there is no guarantee that the other side has received it"
- Disconnected clients buffer events until they reconnect: "buffer events until reconnection"
- The server keeps no such buffer, so events a client missed while offline are not resent after it reconnects.

**Connection drops**
- Packets sent by the client are queued while offline and sent after reconnecting, but an event in flight during the break may still be lost.
- Packets the server emits during the outage are not stored for replay, so the client never receives them.

**At least once**
- *Client to server:* Set the `retries` option (with `ackTimeout`) on the client. The client resends the event until the server acknowledges it, up to `retries + 1` attempts.
- Caveat: "Even in that case, any pending event will be lost if the user refreshes its tab."
- *Server to client:* Socket.IO doesn't provide this. You must build it yourself by giving each event a unique ID, persisting events in a database, and having the client store the last received ID and send it on reconnection so the server can replay missed events.

The page doesn't mention screen lock. The closest statements are from forum posts about switching apps, quoted verbatim below.

**Background (from the original post by Knine9):**
> "Since the upgrade to IOS 15, the WebSocket gets closed after the user gets to another application."

**Background (from wvhn's reply):**
> "When Safari is switched to the background the websocket server recognizes the client going away and closes the websocket."

**Returning to foreground (from wvhn's reply):**
> "When Safari gets to the foreground again, onerror and onclose events are received which allow my site (web-based smart home framework) to re-establish the connection to the websocket server."

**Later caveat (from wvhn's reply):**
> "This may work for hours of inactivity but at some point in time after longer inactivity, the onerror and onclose events will not be received any more. So the site can not recognize the dead connection."

These are user reports, not Apple documentation. The page also notes that turning off the experimental NSURLSession WebSocket option in advanced settings made the connection work again for the original poster.

content.content:
Posted 2020-05-18 (updated the same day).

**Problem:** The author writes, "For some reason, the iOS browser accepted the cert for HTTPS, but not WSS." In other words, iOS trusted the self-signed certificate for secure web pages but rejected secure WebSocket connections.

**Workaround:** The author moved to Socket.IO, "which has a fallback method to HTTPS polling if a websocket connection cannot be established." Socket.IO's polling fallback let the app work on iOS with the self-signed setup.

The post does not mention installing a certificate authority as a fix.

**On self-signed certificates and WebSocket on iOS**

- **Plain self-signed certs:** The author states that "self-signed certs do NOT work for websocket connections." They add that this is "very poorly documented."
- **Failure mode:** Connecting with wss:// to such a server "will result in an empty error."
- **Manual installation:** Installing the certificate by hand does not fix it. The author says, "Manually installing the certificate doesn't help."
- **Recommended workaround:** Create a self-signed CA certificate and install it on the device. Enable full trust for it, then use it to issue the server certificate. The author describes this as "a certificate signed by a dummy CA."
- **iOS versions:** The article does not name any specific iOS version. A commenter says the approach "doesn't work (any more?)" without some changes, and that you "must specify SANs in your ext.conf."

The thread doesn't say anything about iOS 18.x, root CA profiles, or installing a certificate with full trust. There is also no Apple engineer reply. The only participant is the original poster, mackhag.

**The WSS report (verbatim):**

> "We're having trouble connecting to local area network websockets in Safari in the latest iOS26 Beta 3 (iPhone 14), both secure and unsecure. Code works < iOS26 & macOS, etc."

> "Secure behaviour: Error in debug console, even though the certificate has been accepted and the page is loaded as https. Error:"

> WebSocket connection to 'wss://192.168.1.81/api/webSocket' failed: The certificate for this server is invalid. You might be connecting to a server that is pretending to be "192.168.1.81", which could put your confidential information at risk.

**Resolution (verbatim, Aug '25 post):**

> "Seems to be resolved in Beta 5"

**Workaround:** The only workaround mentioned is for the unsecure ws:// case, not WSS: "need to call connectWebSocket() twice, establishes connection reliably. Calling connectWebSocket() once, will sometimes work, sometimes not."

content.thinking: Confirmed that `writable` resets asynchronously, so volatile emits only work for at most one packet per tick: the phone's 30 Hz stream can stay volatile, but the relay-to-scene fan-in and scene-to-HUD fan-out need reliable emits, while per-phone HUD delivery can remain volatile. I'm also dropping connectionStateRecovery to avoid replaying buffered reliable packets, then applying these changes, adding a burst test, and rerunning.

# Netcode: realtime relay, rooms, reconnect, hosting and HTTPS

Target files: `shared/protocol.ts`, `server/rooms.ts`, `server/relay.ts`, `server/index.ts`, `src/net/identity.ts`, `src/net/client.ts`, `src/net/sceneClient.ts`, `src/net/inputHold.ts`, `src/net/qr.ts`, `src/net/scanner.ts`, `tests/relay.test.ts`, `tests/rooms.test.ts`, plus two patches (`vite.config.ts`, `package.json`).

Everything in section 3 was typechecked with the repo's own `tsconfig.json` and `tsconfig.server.json` (strict, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, plus `--noUnusedLocals --noUnusedParameters`), the test suite ran green under vitest 5.0.5 on node 24.15 (16 tests), `server/index.ts` was smoke-run with tsx 4.23 (health, SPA fallback, cache headers), and an 18-phone load test ran through the real relay. Platform claims come from the installed typings/sources under `node_modules` or from the cited pages. Nothing was written inside the repo.

## 0. Evidence index (what was run, what it showed)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Express 5.3.0 route syntax (`proof-express-wildcard.ts`) | `app.get('*')` throws `Missing parameter name at index 1: *`; `/{*splat}` and `/*splat` accepted. Express 5 depends on `router@2.2.0` -> `path-to-regexp@8.4.2`. |
| Socket.IO 4.8.4 relay proof (`proof-relay.ts`) | `io.to(room).emit`, `socket.join([a,b])`, `socket.data`, `emitWithAck`, per-player rooms, `maxHttpBufferSize` (oversize -> ws close code 1009, client `transport close`), `connectionStateRecovery` (`recovered: true` on both ends after `engine.close()`), server `disconnect(true)` -> client `io server disconnect`, `active: false`. |
| vitest 5 pattern (`vitest-proof/`) | server on port 0 + two `socket.io-client` sockets inside `beforeAll`: passes in 236 ms. |
| Vite 8.3.4 bundle of `qrcode` + `qr-scanner` + `socket.io-client` (`vite-proof/`) | builds; `qrcode` resolves to `lib/browser.js` (package `browser` field, Vite `DEFAULT_MAIN_FIELDS` starts with `browser`); qr-scanner's `import("./qr-scanner-worker.min.js")` becomes chunk `qr-scanner-worker.min-*.js` (43.95 kB). |
| Repo `vite.config.ts` as scaffolded | **fails `tsc`**: `TS2769 ... 'test' does not exist in type 'UserConfigExport'`. Fix: `defineConfig` from `vitest/config` (section 3.13). |
| Volatile semantics | read from `engine.io/build/transports/websocket.js` line 63 and `engine.io-client/build/esm/transports/websocket.js` lines 52-73: `writable=false` synchronously on every write, back to true asynchronously. A test with 3 emits in one tick lost 2 of them through a volatile forward; the reliable forward delivers 10/10 in order. |
| Load test (`mirror/loadtest.ts`, localhost) | 18 phones x 30 Hz for 5 s: 2646 sent, 2646 received, 0 % loss; relay hop p50 0.92 ms, p90 2.33 ms, p99 5.80 ms, max 16 ms. HUD fan-out 18 x 10 Hz: 882/882. |
| Payload sizes (JSON) | pilot `in` 78 B, gunner `in` 110 B, engineer `in` 70 B, `hud` 165 B, 18-player `lobby` 1995 B. |

## 1. The problem, in the words of the spec

- "Relay server: a small Node process. Routes messages between phones and the scene by room code. Never does game logic of any kind." (SPEC.md section 1)
- "Inputs flow right at 30 Hz, status flows back at 10 Hz. The relay never runs game logic." (section 11) "Phones send input 30 times per second, not on every sensor event." (section 3)
- "HTTPS everywhere. iOS only grants motion sensors and the camera on secure pages, and only after a user tap." "Zero friction. Scan, tap, play in under 30 seconds. No install, no account." (sections 0-1)
- "It creates a room with a 4-letter code (for example RIVA) and shows a large QR ... The QR encodes https://<host>/play?room=RIVA ... The PLAYER button on the landing page stays as a fallback. It opens an in-app QR scanner plus a field to type the 4-letter code." (section 2)
- "Reconnect: keep a token in localStorage; the same token rejoins the same team and role." "Phones sleeping or dropping: a locked screen kills the connection. Wake lock, plus auto-reconnect into the same slot using the token." (sections 11 and 14)
- "Hosting: relay on the scene PC, exposed with Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000) or ngrok http 3000. Backup host: Render, Railway or Fly.io. Serverless functions are a poor fit for a WebSocket relay." (section 11)
- "Latency: the tunnel adds a round trip. Expect about 50 to 100 ms, fine for this game. Send input at 30 Hz and interpolate." (section 14)
- "Venue WiFi: the tunnel goes over the internet, so guest-network isolation doesn't matter. Backup: phone hotspot for the scene PC, or the backup host." (section 14)
- Messages to keep: `Hello`, `Swap`, `PilotIn`, `GunnerIn` ("dYaw: radians since last packet"), `EngIn`, `Hud`, `Evt` (section 11). Gate 1: "one phone steers a box boat on the TV ... the riskiest unknown."

## 2. Decisions and why

### 2.1 Socket.IO 4.8.4, one namespace, three rooms per game room

- One default namespace `/`. Per game room `CODE`, three Socket.IO rooms: `CODE:scene` (the one scene socket), `CODE:players` (every phone), `CODE:p7` (one phone). `io.to('CODE:scene').emit('in', pid, msg)` is the fan-in; `io.to('CODE:p7').emit('hud', msg)` and `io.to('CODE:players').emit('lobby', msg)` are the fan-outs. `socket.to(...)` (which excludes the sender) is not needed because scene and phones are never in the same target room. Verified against `socket.io/dist/index.d.ts` (`to`, `in`, `except`, `volatile`, `fetchSockets`) and `socket.d.ts` (`join(rooms: Room | Room[])`, `leave`, `data`, `recovered`, `disconnect(close?)`).
- Typed events: `new Server<ClientToServerEvents, ServerToClientEvents, InterServerEvents, SocketData>(httpServer, opts)`; client `io(...)` returns `Socket<ServerToClientEvents, ClientToServerEvents>` (`socket.io-client/build/esm/socket.d.ts`). `emitWithAck` is typed from the ack parameter of the event map; `socket.timeout(ms).emitWithAck(...)` rejects on timeout (`DecorateAcknowledgements`).
- Rejected: raw `ws`. Socket.IO gives rooms, acks, heartbeats, reconnection with backoff, and the HTTP long-polling fallback that turns out to matter on iOS LAN testing (2.11). Rejected: WebRTC data channels (no NAT/TURN work for a hackathon). Rejected: one namespace per room (`io.of(/^\/room-/)`): rooms are enough and keep one connection path through the Vite proxy.

### 2.2 Reliable vs volatile: the one rule that matters

`volatile` means "discard if the transport is not writable right now". That flag is **not** "connected or not": `engine.io/build/transports/websocket.js` sets `this.writable = false` at the top of `send(packets)` and only sets it back in the ws send callback; the browser transport does the same and restores it on `nextTick` (`engine.io-client/build/esm/transports/websocket.js` lines 52-73). `socket.io/dist/client.js` line 173 discards a volatile packet when `!this.conn.transport.writable`; `socket.io-client/build/esm/socket.js` line 263 does the same client-side. Consequence, measured: a loop that emits 18 HUDs, or a relay that forwards inputs from 18 phones arriving in the same tick, keeps the **first** packet and drops the rest if those emits are volatile.

Decision table:

| Leg | Emits per tick per socket | Mode | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| phone -> relay `in` (30 Hz) | 1 | volatile on WebSocket, reliable on polling | one packet per 33 ms; while offline it is dropped, not queued (a queue would burst stale steering on reconnect). On polling the transport is unwritable for a whole round trip, so volatile would discard most packets; reliable lets polling batch them. |
| relay -> scene `in` | up to 18 | **reliable** | fan-in; the volatile window would eat same-tick packets (test "same-tick burst ... complete and in order"). The scene socket is a wired PC; a dead scene is not in the room, so nothing queues. |
| scene -> relay `hud`/`evt` | up to 18 | **reliable** | emitted in a loop in one tick. |
| relay -> phone `hud`/`evt` | 1 | volatile | one per phone per 100 ms; drops rather than queues on a sleeping phone. |
| `lobby`, `room`, `welcome`, `err`, `joined/left/reconnected`, `swap/ready/calibrate/rename/leave`, `gate`, `kick` | rare | reliable | must arrive; each is a snapshot or an edge the other side needs. |

HUD shape decision: **per-player `hud` packets** (165 B, 10 Hz, 1.6 KB/s per phone), not one room broadcast with all players' fields. A broadcast would be ~18 x 150 B = 2.7 KB x 10 Hz x 18 phones = 486 KB/s out of the relay versus 30 KB/s, for no gain: a phone needs only its own fields. `lobby` is the opposite case (everyone needs everyone) and is sent on change only.

### 2.3 `connectionStateRecovery`: off

What it does (verified in `socket.io-adapter/dist/in-memory-adapter.js`, `SessionAwareAdapter`): after an *unexpected* disconnect it keeps the socket's `id`, rooms and `data` plus every **reliable** event (volatile and ack'd events are skipped) for `maxDisconnectionDuration` (default 120 000 ms per the typings) and replays the missed ones when the *same client `Socket` object* reconnects with its `pid`/`offset`. Proof: after `socket.io.engine.close()` both sides reported `recovered: true` and the same `socket.id`. Limits: a page reload creates a new client Socket (no `pid`), so nothing is recovered; a manual `socket.disconnect()` is not stored (docs); the server must have sent at least one event; every reliable packet is appended with a trailing offset argument (seen as `'Q54Uz54'` in the proof); with our reliable `in` forward it would store ~540 packets/s for two minutes and replay stale inputs. The 30-second phone sleep is handled by the token re-join instead (2.4), which also survives reloads and relay restarts. Rejected: enabling it with a short window; the extra argument and replay semantics buy nothing we need.

### 2.4 Identity and reconnect

- Phone token: `crypto.randomUUID()` in `localStorage` (`gr.playerToken`). `randomUUID` exists only in secure contexts (MDN), and a plain-http LAN test page has none, so `getRandomValues` (works in insecure contexts, MDN) builds a v4 UUID as fallback. Storage access is try/catch'd (Safari private mode).
- Relay maps token -> (room, pid) in `RoomRegistry`. `hello` with a known token re-attaches the new socket to the same pid and tells the scene `reconnected`; the scene owns the roster (team, role, ready, calibrated) and simply flips `connected`. `hello` is sent on **every** `connect`, so it is idempotent and independent of Socket.IO internals.
- Second device with the same token (duplicated tab): newest socket wins, the old one gets `err replaced` and is detached (test "rejoins the same slot").
- Player disconnect vs leave: a transport close keeps the slot for `NET.playerGraceMs` (10 min, longer than a match) and the scene gets `left {reason:'disconnect'}` (it shows "phone dropped" and keeps the seat); `leave` frees the slot immediately (`left {reason:'leave'}`); `kick` from the scene does the same plus `err kicked` to the phone; a slot that stays disconnected past the grace is `left {reason:'expired'}`.
- Scene: `sessionStorage['gr.scene'] = {code, sceneToken}`. On reload it sends `host {code, sceneToken}`; the relay re-claims if the room is still alive and the token matches, answers `room {reclaimed:true, players:[...]}` and tells phones `room {sceneOnline:true}`. A wrong token or an expired room answers `no_room`, and the client clears the session and hosts a fresh room (new code, new QR). Grace: `NET.sceneGraceMs` = 90 s (long enough for a Vite full reload or a laptop lid flap, short enough that a crashed scene does not hold phones hostage). Meanwhile phones get `room {sceneOnline:false}` (show "Big screen reconnecting..."), inputs still flow but have no receiver. After the grace the relay sends `err room_closed` to every phone in the room, detaches them and deletes the room. A duplicated scene tab shares `sessionStorage`; a re-claim therefore replaces the previous scene socket (`err replaced`), so inputs never fan out to two scenes.
- The scene also needs its roster to survive its own reload: persist the pid -> seat map in `sessionStorage` from the lobby code (Track A phone/lobby work), and rebuild it from `room.players` on `reclaimed`.

### 2.5 Room codes

4 letters from `ABCDEFGHJKMNPRSTUVWXYZ` (no I, L, O, Q: they read as 1/l, I, 0, O on a projector), unique per server (the registry checks). Generated as consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel from `BCDFGHJKMNPRSTVWXYZ` x `AEU` (3249 combinations, pronounceable: "DAMU", "SETA"), with a small blocklist, falling back to any 4 letters from the alphabet after 64 collisions (234 256 codes). Note: the spec's example "RIVA" contains I and is therefore not a valid code here; "DAMA" is. Input is upper-cased and trimmed; `roomCodeFromText` also accepts a pasted `/play?room=DAMA` link.

### 2.6 Gate: full room, match running, late joiners

The relay must answer "room full" and "match running" without knowing the game, so the scene sends a tiny `gate {max, locked, late}` whenever it changes (team size change, start, end). Unknown token + `players.size >= max` -> `err room_full`. Unknown token while `locked` -> `welcome {queued:true}` and `joined {queued:true}` to the scene (which seats them as spectator until the next lobby) when `late:'queue'`, or `err match_running` when `late:'reject'`. Known tokens always re-join, locked or not. Default gate: `max: 18, locked: false, late: 'queue'`.

### 2.7 Rate and flow control

- Phones: `setInterval(1000/30)`, one packet per tick built by a sampler the phone UI supplies; `seq` is assigned by the net client. Browsers throttle timers in background tabs, which is fine: a backgrounded phone cannot play.
- Relay per socket: token bucket 45 inputs/s with burst 60 (a 30 Hz phone never trips it; a runaway loop does), 10 control messages/s (`hello/host/swap/ready/calibrate/rename`) with `err rate_limited` on excess. `maxHttpBufferSize: 8192` closes the connection on any single message above 8 KB (engine.io default is 1 MB); our largest message, an 18-player roster, is ~2 KB.
- Validation: `parseInput` checks `t`, `role`, finite numbers, clamps `steer` to [-1, 1], `dYaw` to [-pi, pi], `yaw` to +-64 pi, `shake` to [0, 1], coerces booleans with `=== true`, normalises `use` to `0 | 1 | null`, and drops anything else. Names: control characters stripped, 16 chars max.
- HUD: the scene calls `startHudLoop(collect)` at 10 Hz; one reliable `hud` per player per tick to the relay, volatile from the relay to each phone. Roster `lobby`: on change, reliable, full snapshot.
- Scene-side hold: `InputHold.offer` keeps the last packet per pid, drops `seq <= last` unless it jumped back by more than 1000 (phone reload), and `read()` reports `dropped: ageMs > 1500` so the HUD shows "phone dropped" and the sim keeps applying the last known gas/steer (a boat that coasts straight is better than one that stops dead).

### 2.8 `dYaw`: deltas versus absolute yaw

The spec defines `dYaw` as radians since the last packet. Deltas are exactly what volatile delivery breaks: every dropped packet is rotation lost forever, and 30 Hz over a tunnel with a sleeping tab will drop packets. Decision: keep the field name and meaning, but make the sim use two added fields:

- `yaw`: the phone's accumulated aim angle since its last calibrate/recenter (already gain-applied and dead-zoned). Absolute, so any packet alone is enough: `aimWorld = base + yaw`.
- `ep`: an epoch counter the phone increments on calibrate/recenter. When the scene sees `ep` change it re-bases: `base = bowHeading - yaw`, which puts the aim behind the bow at that instant (the spec's "reset behind the bow"). This is robust to a lost `recenter: true` packet; `recenter` is kept for the HUD flash only.
- `dYaw` stays for logging, drift tests and as a turn-rate hint for the aim-assist gain drop.
- Same idea for edges: `fc` counts fire taps (a 20 ms tap can fall between two 33 ms packets), `uc` counts power uses and the phone latches `use` for ~5 packets; `AimTracker.takeFireTap` / `takeUse` apply each tap exactly once.

Rejected: TCP-reliable deltas (no drops but a 2-minute replay burst after a sleep, and the relay would have to queue for dead phones); server-side integration (the relay would interpret game data).

### 2.9 Heartbeat

Server `pingInterval: 10000, pingTimeout: 10000` (engine.io defaults 25 000 / 20 000). The server pings; the client closes if no ping arrives within `pingInterval + pingTimeout` (Socket.IO docs). So a vanished phone is `left` on the scene within 20 s, and a phone wakes up and notices its dead link within 20 s at worst. The 10 s ping also keeps Cloudflare's WebSocket idle timeout (documented as "a period of time", widely reported as ~100 s) from closing quiet connections. The InputHold's 1.5 s rule covers the HUD; the heartbeat only drives relay bookkeeping. `PhoneClient` additionally forces a fresh transport on `visibilitychange -> visible` when no ping was seen for two intervals (iOS reports that `onclose` sometimes never fires after long background time).

### 2.10 Express 5, static, SPA fallback, tsx

- Express 5 uses `path-to-regexp` 8: `'*'` throws; the wildcard needs a name, and braces make it optional so it also matches `/`: `app.get('/{*splat}', ...)` (Express migration guide, proven). `/api/*` and `/socket.io/*` are answered 404 inside the fallback so a typo never returns `index.html` as JSON. Socket.IO attaches to the `http.Server` itself and intercepts `/socket.io` before Express.
- `express.static(dist/assets, { immutable: true, maxAge: '1y' })` for hashed assets, `express.static(dist, { index: false, maxAge: 0 })` for the rest, and `res.sendFile(index.html, { headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-store' } })` so phones always fetch the newest build (measured headers in section 0). Without `dist/` the server answers 503 with the dev-mode hint.
- `/api/health` returns `{ok, uptimeSec, rooms, players, sockets, dist}` (`io.engine.clientsCount`).
- `tsx watch server/index.ts` in dev (already in `package.json`), `NODE_ENV=production tsx server/index.ts` in prod. tsx reads the root `tsconfig.json` `paths`, so `@shared/protocol.ts` resolves at runtime (smoke-run proved it). For a backup host, move `tsx` to `dependencies` (section 3.14), because a production `npm install` skips devDependencies.
- CORS: not configured. In dev the phone talks to Vite on 5173, which proxies `/socket.io` with `ws: true` to 3000 (same origin); in prod Express serves the app and the socket on one port. `allowRequest` optionally restricts the `Origin` header (`ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://x.trycloudflare.com`); leave it empty for the demo.

### 2.11 Hosting and HTTPS

**Cloudflare quick tunnel (primary).** `brew install cloudflared` (Cloudflare downloads page), then `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:5173` (dev, `npm run tunnel`) or `--url http://localhost:3000` (prod, `npm run tunnel:prod`). Each run gets a new random `*.trycloudflare.com` hostname; no account. Documented limits: 200 in-flight requests (HTTP 429 above), no Server-Sent Events, no uptime guarantee. WebSockets: Cloudflare proxies WebSockets on all plans with no configuration; a third-party guide tested a WebSocket server through a quick tunnel and reports Socket.IO and Vite HMR work. Connect time: the URL prints within seconds, but the name resolves 3-33 s later (measured by the same guide), so start the tunnel before opening the scene. Keep the 10 s ping (2.9) for the idle timeout. Rejected as primary: named tunnels (need an account and a domain; fine if someone has one, they also remove the 200-request cap).

**ngrok free (fallback).** `ngrok http 5173`. Free plan shows an interstitial "You are about to visit..." page in front of HTML browser traffic; it is skipped only by sending the `ngrok-skip-browser-warning` request header (any value) or a custom User-Agent, which a QR scan into Safari cannot do. Consequence: every phone taps "Visit Site" once, then a 7-day cookie suppresses it for that domain; API/WebSocket requests are not affected, so the socket works after that tap. The free plan also gives one static dev domain (stable QR between runs), 1 GB/month, 20 000 HTTP requests/month, 4 000 req/min, 3 endpoints. Acceptable as a backup; the extra tap is why cloudflared is first.

**Vite dev through the tunnel.** `server.allowedHosts` must include the tunnel host (`.trycloudflare.com`, `.ngrok-free.app`) or Vite answers 403 "Blocked request"; `true` works but disables the DNS-rebinding check. HMR: the HMR client connects back to the page host; through a 443 tunnel set `server.ws = { protocol: 'wss', host: TUNNEL_HOST, clientPort: 443 }` (Vite 8 types: `server.hmr.{protocol,host,port,clientPort,path,timeout,server}` are `@deprecated Use server.ws.*`, still auto-synced; `WsOptions` has `protocol, host, port, clientPort, path, timeout, server`). Phones never need HMR; only the scene PC does, and it can simply use `http://localhost:5173`. The `/socket.io` proxy uses `ws: true` (`ProxyOptions.ws`). Alternative without config: `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:5173 --http-host-header localhost:5173`.

**Production path.** `npm run build && npm start` then `npm run tunnel:prod`: one port, Express serves `dist/`, Socket.IO on the same server, no proxy, no HMR. This is the demo configuration.

**LAN HTTPS with `@vitejs/plugin-basic-ssl` (and why it half-works on iPhone).** The plugin creates a self-signed certificate (not a CA). WebKit decides "secure context" from scheme and host only (`SecurityOrigin.cpp`: `shouldTreatAsPotentiallyTrustworthy` checks the secure-scheme registry, `localhost`, loopback; it never inspects the certificate; the W3C Secure Contexts spec says `https`/`wss` -> potentially trustworthy, with no certificate-error clause). So after the user taps through "This Connection Is Not Private", the page *is* a secure context and `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` (secure context + transient activation, MDN) is available. What does **not** work: `wss://` to that same host. iOS Safari accepts the page certificate but refuses WebSocket connections to a self-signed server ("For some reason, the iOS browser accepted the cert for HTTPS, but not WSS", 2020; a widely-shared gist: "self-signed certs do NOT work for websocket connections ... Manually installing the certificate doesn't help"; Apple forum on iOS 26 beta: `wss://192.168.1.81/...` "The certificate for this server is invalid" after the page loaded). The mitigation is in the client: `transports: ['websocket', 'polling'], tryAllTransports: true`, because `engine.io-client` only moves to the next transport on error when `tryAllTransports` is set (`socket.js` `_onError`, lines 596-601); the polling fallback is plain HTTPS XHR, which honours the accepted certificate, and the input loop switches to reliable emits on polling (2.2). Expect polling on LAN to add one RTT (~5-20 ms) of jitter: fine for Gate 1, not what you demo with.

**mkcert (proper LAN HTTPS).** `brew install mkcert && mkcert -install && mkcert 192.168.1.23 localhost`, then `vite --https` with `server.https = { key, cert }` instead of basic-ssl. On the iPhone: AirDrop `$(mkcert -CAROOT)/rootCA.pem`, Settings > Profile Downloaded > Install, then Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings > enable full trust (mkcert README). With a trusted CA, `wss://` works and WebSocket is used. One known problem: on some iOS 18 builds the installed CA does not appear in the trust settings. Budget 10 minutes per phone; only worth it if the venue has no internet.

**Backup hosts.** Render Free: web services spin down after 15 minutes with no inbound HTTP request *or WebSocket message on an existing connection* (changelog 2026-02-24), wake on the next request in about one minute, 750 free instance hours/month, may restart at any time; our 10 s pings count as WebSocket messages, so a live room never sleeps. Railway: Free Trial with a one-time $5 credit for 30 days, no credit card; Free plan with $1/month credit; Hobby $5/month; no spin-down. Fly.io: no free tier for new organisations (trial of 2 machine-hours or 7 days), cheapest always-on machine $2.19 per 30 days; machines can auto-stop when idle. Pick: **Render Free** as the no-card, documented option; wake it 10 minutes before the demo by opening `/api/health`. Recipe: push the repo to GitHub; Render > New > Web Service > connect the repo; Runtime Node; Build command `npm ci && npm run build`; Start command `npm start`; Health check path `/api/health`; no env vars needed (`PORT` is injected and `server/index.ts` reads it; `HOST` defaults to `0.0.0.0`); move `tsx` to `dependencies` first (3.14); deploy, open `https://<service>.onrender.com/scene`, and the QR encodes that origin automatically. For Railway it is the same build/start pair with `PORT` injected.

### 2.12 Latency, ordering, no prediction

- Budget through a tunnel: phone -> Cloudflare edge -> cloudflared on the PC. The spec expects 50-100 ms RTT; the relay itself adds ~1 ms (p50 0.92 ms, p99 5.8 ms measured). End to end: half a sample interval (16 ms) + one way (25-50 ms) + relay (1 ms) + up to one sim step (16 ms) + one frame (16 ms): roughly 75-100 ms glass-to-glass. Steering and gas are continuous and the boat has inertia, so this is below what players feel; gyro aim at gain 2 is where latency shows, which is why aim assist exists in the spec.
- Why 30 Hz plus hold is enough: the sim runs at 60 Hz and reads the held packet every step, so a 30 Hz stream is sampled twice; no interpolation of inputs is needed (positions are interpolated by the renderer, not inputs).
- No client prediction: phones never render the world; there is nothing to predict and nothing to reconcile. The only phone-side feedback (steering-wheel graphic, compass needle) is local and immediate.
- Ordering and staleness: `seq` per input packet, assigned by the client. Socket.IO guarantees ordering on one connection, but after a reconnect or on the polling fallback the scene can receive an old packet after a newer one from the previous connection; `InputHold` drops `seq <= last`. No clock sync: there are no timestamps on the wire; the relay stamps nothing; staleness is measured by arrival time on the scene.
- RTT on screen: the phone can show `await socket.timeout(2000).emitWithAck('hello', ...)` round-trip time in its debug footer; cheap and useful at the venue.

## 4. Edge cases and how each is handled

| # | Case | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Phone sleeps 30 s (screen lock, app switch) | iOS kills the socket; on wake the throttled ping timer fires -> reconnect (500 ms..3 s backoff) -> `hello` with the same token -> `welcome {rejoined:true}` -> scene `reconnected` -> scene re-sends `lobby` and the next `hud`. `visibilitychange` forces a fresh transport if no ping was seen for 20 s. Inputs while away were volatile: nothing bursts. |
| 2 | Phone page reload / Safari tab killed | Token in `localStorage` -> same pid. `seq` restarts at 1; `InputHold` accepts the jump because it is > 1000 below the last seq. |
| 3 | Same token on two devices (duplicated tab) | Newest socket wins; old gets `err replaced` and leaves its rooms. Server-side `disconnect` of the old socket does not detach the slot because `player.socketId !== socket.id`. |
| 4 | Private browsing (no `localStorage`) | New token per load -> new slot per reload. Acceptable; phone shows its pid/team again. |
| 5 | Scene reload (Vite full reload, F5) | `sessionStorage` -> `host {code, sceneToken}` -> `reclaimed:true` with the player list; phones saw `room {sceneOnline:false}` then `{true}`. |
| 6 | Scene away longer than 90 s / scene PC crash | Room closed; phones get `err room_closed`, UI returns to the join screen; a scene that comes back gets `no_room`, creates a new room, shows a new QR. |
| 7 | Duplicated scene tab re-claims the room | Previous scene socket gets `err replaced` and leaves `CODE:scene`; inputs go to one scene only (tested). |
| 8 | Relay restart | All rooms gone (in-memory by design). Scene: `no_room` -> new room. Phones: `no_room` on hello -> "scan the new QR". Run the relay under `tsx watch` only in dev; in prod keep it in a terminal you do not touch. |
| 9 | Room full | `err room_full` from the gate (`max` set by the scene from team size x 6). |
| 10 | Join during a match | `welcome {queued:true}`; scene seats as spectator until the next lobby. With `late:'reject'`: `err match_running`. |
| 11 | Old cached phone page after a deploy | `auth.v` mismatch -> middleware error -> client `connect_error` with `data.code = 'bad_version'` -> "Reload the page". |
| 12 | Oversized or malformed message | > 8 KB closes the connection (ws code 1009, proven); junk fails the parsers and is dropped; NaN/Infinity rejected; numbers clamped. |
| 13 | Runaway client loop | Inputs above 45/s dropped silently (logged once per 300); control messages above 10/s answered `err rate_limited`. |
| 14 | Lost input packet | Last packet held; gas/steer are states, `yaw` is absolute, `ep`/`fc`/`uc` counters make recenter/fire/use idempotent. |
| 15 | No input for 1.5 s | `InputHold.read().dropped` -> HUD "phone dropped" badge; the sim keeps the last state. |
| 16 | Out-of-order / stale after reconnect | `seq` monotonic; `InputHold` ignores `seq <= last`. |
| 17 | iOS on self-signed LAN cert | Page is a secure context; `wss://` fails; `tryAllTransports` falls back to polling; inputs switch to reliable emits on polling. |
| 18 | Venue WiFi blocks WebSocket | Same fallback: HTTPS long-polling through the tunnel. |
| 19 | Scene PC opened on `localhost:5173` while phones use the tunnel | `joinUrl` would encode localhost; `joinUrlLooksLocal()` lets the scene UI warn; set `VITE_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://x.trycloudflare.com` or open the scene through the tunnel URL. |
| 20 | Tunnel URL changes between runs | QR is generated at runtime from `location.origin`; nothing is hard-coded. |
| 21 | ngrok interstitial | One "Visit Site" tap per phone per 7 days; socket traffic unaffected. |
| 22 | Cloudflare/ngrok idle timeout | 10 s server pings keep every socket active. |
| 23 | Cloudflare 200 in-flight request cap | 18 phones + 1 scene = 19 sockets (one upgrade request each); polling fallback adds one in-flight request per phone; far below 200. |
| 24 | Two scenes on one relay (two rooms) | Rooms are isolated by code; the registry is per server; codes unique. |
| 25 | `/api/typo` or `/socket.io/x` on prod | 404 from the fallback, never `index.html`. |
| 26 | Build missing in prod | 503 with the hint; `/api/health.dist === false`. |
| 27 | Name edits | `rename` updates the registry and the scene; names sanitised to 16 printable chars. |
| 28 | Kick from the scene UI | `kick(pid)` -> slot freed, phone gets `err kicked`, scene gets `left {reason:'kick'}`. |
| 29 | Explicit leave then re-scan | Slot freed; the next `hello` is a fresh join with a new pid. |

## 1. The problem, in the words of the spec

- "Relay server: a small Node process. Routes messages between phones and the scene by room code. Never does game logic of any kind." (SPEC.md section 1)
- "Inputs flow right at 30 Hz, status flows back at 10 Hz. The relay never runs game logic." (section 11) "Phones send input 30 times per second, not on every sensor event." (section 3)
- "HTTPS everywhere. iOS only grants motion sensors and the camera on secure pages, and only after a user tap." "Zero friction. Scan, tap, play in under 30 seconds. No install, no account." (sections 0-1)
- "It creates a room with a 4-letter code (for example RIVA) and shows a large QR ... The QR encodes https://<host>/play?room=RIVA ... The PLAYER button on the landing page stays as a fallback. It opens an in-app QR scanner plus a field to type the 4-letter code." (section 2)
